item.title: Sheehan switches to number eight for Munster derby
item.description: Dan Sheehan will captain Ireland in next month's Nations Championship games in Caelan Doris' absence [Getty Images] Leinster captain Dan Sheehan will start at number eight for the first time in Saturday's United Rugby Championship derby against Munster in Dublin. The Ireland hooker switches to the back row as one of four changes made by head coach Leo Cullen for the Aviva Stadium game (18:00 BST) following last weekend's 48-23 Investec Champions Cup victory over Clermont Auvergne. Ireland scrum-half Jamison Gibson-Park makes his first appearance of the season, while former Munster out-half Joey Carbery earns his first start since rejoining Leinster. Ronan Kelleher and Jamie Osborne are also drafted into the starting side, with Kelleher replacing Sheehan at hooker and Osborne joining Robbie Henshaw in midfield. The hosts are seeking consecutive URC victories after bouncing back from opening defeats by the Lions and Sharks with a convincing win over Cardiff. Leinster have collected eight points from their opening three league matches, including four bonus points. Munster, meanwhile, have made seven changes to the side that defeated Racing 92 in the Champions Cup last weekend. Shane Daly returns from injury, while Josh Wycherley, Kieran Brookes, Fineen Wycherley, Jack O'Donoghue, Alex Kendellen and Gavin Coombes are also drafted into the starting XV. Former Ireland Under-20 international Sean O'Brien switches from the wing to outside centre as he prepares to make his 50th Munster appearance. Mark Donnelly is in line for his first appearance of the season from the replacements' bench, with academy centre Gordon Wood also among the replacements. Tadhg Beirne and Craig Casey - the only Munster players in Andy Farrell's latest Ireland squad - both start. Munster have recovered from their opening URC defeat by Glasgow Warriors with a victory over the Bulls and a 26-26 draw against Ulster on October 10. Line-ups Leinster: Keenan; T O'Brien, Osborne, Henshaw, J O'Brien; Carbery, Gibson-Park; Porter, Kelleher, Furlong; J McCarthy, Ryan; Baird, Van der Flier, Sheehan (capt). Replacements: G McCarthy, Usanov, Clarkson, O'Tighearnaigh, Penny, Gunne, Gabriel, Tector. Munster: B O'Connor; McCarthy, S O'Brien, Nankivell, Daly; O'Shea, Casey; J Wycherley, Van der Merwe, Brookes; F Wycherley, Beirne (capt); O'Donoghue, Kendellen, Coombes. Replacements: Clein, Donnelly, Ala'alatoa, Edogbo, Gleeson, B O'Donovan, Hanrahan, Wood.

item.title: Los Angeles Chargers news: Omarion Hampton still ranked highly among 2nd-year backs
item.description: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - OCTOBER 18: Linebacker Nick Bolton #32 of the Kansas City Chiefs tackles running back Omarion Hampton #8 of the Los Angeles Chargers in the second quarter at Arrowhead Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s been a rough season thus far for Omarion Hampton. He was supposed to be one of the best young backs in the league. NFL insider Jordan Schultz at one point made a bold prediction that Hampton would lead the NFL in scrimmage yards while finishing with 12+ touchdowns. He’s currently barely on pace for that amount of touchdowns and you can’t lead the league in yards from scrimmage if you are barely on the field. That’s what it’s been like for the 23-year old who came into the league with the expectation that he’d be a lead guy for a team. Hard to imagine he’s in any kind of good spirits since the two lost fumbles in the first two weeks of this season. But despite that, outside of the team, there are believers. Take Bleacher Report’s Gary Davenport who just recently re-ranked the second-year backs in the league. Hampton came in third, behind only Ashton Jeanty and TreyVeon Henderson. “ Omarion Hampton has had little opportunity to establish a rhythm. ” “ When the 23-year-old was drafted 22nd overall last year, it was with the expectation that he would be the Chargers’ lead back from the jump. He was widely considered a first-round talent after a wildly productive two-season stretch at North Carolina. ” “ An ankle injury sidelined Hampton for almost half his rookie season, but he was effective when available. He averaged 4.4 yards per carry, scored five touchdowns and contributed just under 82 total yards per game. Then 2026 rolled around, and the wheels came off. ” “The winless Chargers are a mess, and Mike McDaniel’s decision to use a three-back committee has done little to help Hampton find his groove. Hampton has exceeded 15 carries just once this season, while his yards-per-carry average has dropped by nearly a full yard. ” “ The talent is there, but the situation is a nightmare. ” Do you think Davenport is correct to still hold Hampton in such high regard? Should he be lower based on his current situation? Let us know below! And now for today’s links. item.title: Maryland staffer called cops on student journalists reporting on Mike Locksley firing
item.description: Tommy Gilligan-Imagn Images Maryland staffer called cops on student journalists reporting on Mike Locksley firing appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . Maryland football decided to move on from Mike Locksley on Wednesday. Locksley was fired after dropping to 2-5 this season and 39-54 overall as head coach, which included an interim stint back in 2015. In the aftermath of the termination, student journalists for the Testudo Times, the student-run Maryland athletic news site, were questioned by police , per a post by Nolan Rogalski of the Testudo Times. “For @testudotimes, @JudeWilkenfeld and I were outside Jones-Hill House trying to get players to comment. An athletics staffer took pictures of us, and a police dispatch was called for suspicious activity; a cop and 2 cop cars pulled up, and officers ID’d us and asked us to leave,” the post from Rogalski on X, formerly Twitter, read. Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) The students appeared not to be causing harm nor doing anything that would be deemed illegal. It is unknown why the staffer called the police. Still, it is common practice for student-run news affiliates to try to get comments after a coach is let go. Last season, by this point in October, seven coaches had already been fired, and in most cases, student-run news outlets tried to get comments. A spokesperson on behalf of the University of Maryland Police Department and Maryland Athletics released a statement regarding the interaction . “UMPD was contacted today, October 21, 2026, about two individuals who were standing outside of Jones Hill House. Due to heightened concerns for staff and player safety around the football program in recent weeks, there has been increased security around athletics facilities. A UMPD officer approached the two individuals, learned they were with a campus media organization, recorded student IDs, and no report was taken. UMPD and Maryland Athletics respect the First Amendment rights of all journalists reporting in public spaces,” the statement read. Maryland is off this week as they move to their interim coach. Their next game is a home date against Illinois on October 31. item.title: Jurgen Klopp picks Barcelona over Real Madrid ahead of crucial El Clasico: ‘I support the better team’
item.description: Jurgen Klopp picks Barcelona over Real Madrid ahead of crucial El Clasico: ‘I support the better team’ Jurgen Klopp believes Barcelona are currently the stronger side ahead of Sunday’s El Clasico, backing Hansi Flick’s team to have the edge over Real Madrid despite their contrasting results in the Champions League. The German head coach will be watching the showdown at Spotify Camp Nou , where Barcelona can strengthen their position at the top of La Liga and extend their six-point advantage over their fiercest rivals with a victory. The former Liverpool manager also revealed why he used to favour Barcelona when watching the rivalry, pointing to his dislike of Real Madrid’s defensive approach during the era of Pepe. Klopp now considers himself a neutral observer, but his assessment of the teams’ current levels gives Barcelona a strong endorsement ahead of a fixture that could have a significant impact on the title race. Klopp explains why he favours Barcelona over Real Madrid Klopp confirmed that El Clasico remains a fixture he has followed throughout his life, regardless of where he has been working. Jurgen Klopp has backed Barcelona for El Clasico. (Photo by Maja Hitij/Getty Images) His historical preference for Barcelona, however, was shaped by his reaction to the way Madrid defended during some of the rivalry’s most intense encounters. “Of course I’ll watch El Clasico between Barcelona and Real Madrid. I’ve watched this game at every stage of my life. “In the past, I was more of a Barcelona supporter because I used to hate it when Pepe and the other defenders used to clear everything out of the way back then. “That’s the only reason I always supported Barça. These days, I watch it with a neutral perspective. “Today, I support the better team. And looking at things at the moment, that is probably Barcelona,” he told Buli News . Barcelona face Real Madrid with six-point lead at stake Barcelona are the favourites to beat Real Madrid. (Photo by Franco Arland/Getty Images) Barcelona enter the Clasico six points ahead of Real Madrid, giving the contest added importance. A home victory would allow Flick’s side to increase that margin and put further pressure on their rivals early in the campaign. However, Barcelona’s preparations have not been entirely straightforward, as their first defeat of the season came against Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League, with the French side exposing defensive weaknesses and securing a 4-2 victory. Real Madrid, by contrast, head into the weekend after beating RB Leipzig 4-1 in Europe. That result offers the visitors a confidence boost and presents a different picture from the league standings, where Barcelona hold the advantage.

item.title: Elephant Rumblings: Kotsay Staying Put?
item.description: CLEVELAND, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 20: Umpire Stu Scheurwater #85 argues with manager Mark Kotsay #7 of the Athletics after Kotsay was ejected during the third inning against the Cleveland Guardians at Progressive Field on September 20, 2026, in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Happy Thursday everyone! The World Series is nearly upon us. Just one more day before baseball fans are treated to Game 1 of the Fall Classic between the Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays. Neither team has won the World Series so one way or another, one organization is going to taste the sweet feeling of hoisting the Commissioner’s Trophy within the next two weeks. And for A’s fans, there aren’t any major former Athletics on these teams (sorry Jorge Mateo and Chad Patrick ). Still, there is a sense of comradery among the fanbases. Tampa and Milwaukee have been low-spenders for the majority of their existences, much like the Athletics. Getting to watch one of these low-payroll franchises lift that final trophy will be awesome to watch for A’s fans. A remind that even against the highest-spending teams like the Dodgers and Yankees, any team can win on any day in baseball. Anyway, now that the A’s have their top voice in the front office, it’s time for Taylor Smith to begin staffing that office. And that’s something that the team is starting on immediately. And based off the comments from yesterday’s presser, it sounds like Smith will be hiring a GM to work under him. That’s not a shock considering that’s how most front offices work in baseball these days. Now we have to see who Smith will tab as his second-in-command. Furthermore, from that same presser it sounds like manager Mark Kotsay’s job is safe, at least for now: Taylor Smith and A’s manager Mark Kotsay will have dinner tonight in Vegas. Smith: “From my conversations with Mark so far, he seems like a great guy. Someone who's hungry for all the information we can get [the coaching staff], and I think it'll be a great partnership.” — Martín Gallegos (@MartinJGallegos) October 21, 2026 That doesn’t sound like someone who is getting ready to make a change in the dugout. There wasn’t a huge expectation that Kotsay would be given his walking papers after the hiring of the next POBO but it was still a possibility. Based off those comments we can expect to see Kotsay in the dugout this spring. How long he lasts will depend on how quickly the team can begin turning things around. No baseball today but the World Series tomorrow! Have a great Friday Junior A’s fans. item.title: Charles Davalan singles, plus Brent Honeywell Jr. in Dominican Winter League
item.description: Oct 18, 2024; New York City, New York, USA; Los Angeles Dodgers relief pitcher Brent Honeywell (40) reacts during the fourth inning of game five of the NLCS against the New York Mets during the 2024 MLB playoffs at Citi Field. Mandatory Credit: Brad Penner-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con Wednesday was light in Dodgers action in the Arizona Fall League, as the Glendale Desert Dogs were shut out in a game shortened by rain to only six innings. Against the Peoria Javelinas, Glendale managed only four hits, all singles, one of them by second baseman Charles Davalan. So let’s expand our offseason minor league scope a bit, and turn to the Dominican Winter League (or LIDOM, if you prefer). As far as I can tell, shortstop Emil Morales is the only Dodgers minor leaguer currently active in the league, which started its season last Friday. item.title: Nick Wright just doubled down on his ‘phenomenal’ Angel Reese take after watching WNBA Finals Game 3
item.description: Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Nick Wright has been left impressed with what he has seen from Angel Reese during the 2026 WNBA Finals so far. After Game 3, which took place on Wednesday, Reese became the first player in league history to drop three consecutive triple-doubles in her first three Finals games and is the youngest player in WNBA Finals history to record three straight double-doubles. Meanwhile, Nick Wright said ahead of Wednesday’s action that Reese has been phenomenal this year and her performances this postseason are giving her the opportunity to be one of the league’s best players behind A’ja Wilson. Prior to Game 3, Wright said: “If Angel Reese was going to have her status as a player stay at the level of her status as a celebrity, she needed to get better. It felt like her game had stagnated, if not dipped. Well, this year, that changed considerably; she’s been phenomenal. “Angel Reese’s performances these playoffs, as she might have her team on the doorstep of a championship, give her the opportunity to be right alongside, I’ll call it a step behind, A’ja Wilson as the top player in the sport.” Now, after the Atlanta Dream’s latest win, he has taken to X to quote the video of himself saying the above. He doubled down on his praise, listing off her impressive resume, describing it as a ‘Helluva portfolio’ while saying she is one game away from being the 2026 WNBA Finals MVP. He wrote: “Angel Reese is one game away from adding a Finals MVP trophy to go alongside her DPOY trophy, college National Championship trophy, NCAA Tournament MOP trophy. Helluva portfolio.” The Dream won Game 3 97-71, with Reese leading the game in scoring (21 points). item.description: PASADENA, CA - OCTOBER 17: Wisconsin Badgers head coach Luke Fickell during the game between the UCLA Bruins and the Wisconsin Badgers on October 17, 2026 at Rose Bowl Stadium in Pasadena. (Photo by David Dennis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NCAA. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Wisconsin fans and fans across the country. Coming off a 17-7 loss to the UCLA Bruins, the Wisconsin Badgers will have to bounce back quickly against another West Coast team, as they take on the USC Trojans at Camp Randall Stadium this weekend. Coming into the game, the Badgers are 2.5-point underdogs at home, facing a Trojans team with an explosive offense that has gone 6-1 thus far. However, many of USC’s wins to date have been uninspiring. They’re on a two-game win streak following their loss to Oregon, but they’ve played two disappointing teams in Washington and Penn State quite closely (25-21 and 31-23). Apart from that, they also had a close 42-35 win over Rutgers and a few early-season wins where they won more comfortably, but the defense was exposed as a problem in the second half. Despite switching coordinators, the Trojans continue to have problems defensively, and Lincoln Riley has been on many hot seat lists, even with his supposed $70+ million buyout. So this game is huge for both sides: the Badgers need a win to get back on the right track, while the Trojans can’t afford a loss in their hope of a College Football Playoff appearance. item.title: 2026-27 Ivy League Men’s Basketball Preview
item.description: ALLSTON, MA - OCTOBER 14: A close up view of the Ivy League logo on a basketball during Harvard Crimson Madness on October 14, 2022, at Lavietes Pavilion in Allston, MA. (Photo by Erica Denhoff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After years of the same eight coaches, there have been five coaching changes in the last three seasons of Ivy League basketball. Fran McCaffery made waves by winning Ivy Madness in year one at Penn last season. Can the Quakers go back-to-back? Harvard and Yale have vengeance on their minds after overtime losses to the Quakers in Ithaca. Princeton returns its entire team. Cornell looks to get over the hump, while Columbia, Dartmouth and Brown look for breakthroughs under their second- and first-year coaches. 1. PENN WHAT I LIKE: The Quakers return most of their rotation pieces from the squad that shocked the world and won Ivy Madness last year. That all starts with TJ Power, whose 44-point miracle performance against Yale stands as one of the league’s greatest ever. He’s a legit three-level scoring superstar in the Ivy League, and at 6-foot-8, he’s a mismatch nightmare for opponents. One of the league’s deadliest shooters, Mike Zanoni, returns alongside him. Notre Dame transfer Sir Mohammed adds a little bit of physicality on the wing, something that Penn desperately needs. There’s depth in the frontcourt with the returning Dalton Scantlebury/Augie Gerhart duo. Both are skilled post scorers, and I think Scantlebury could eventually leapfrog Gerhart in the rotation. Lucas Lueth also gives the Quakers some rim protection and athleticism up front, although he’s more a four than five. WHAT I DON’T LIKE: Penn’s analytical profile relies a ton on mid-range jump shots. The Quakers didn’t get to the rim at a high enough rate last year and are one of the few teams that still consistently runs actions for long twos. Penn will have the same strengths and weaknesses as last season. That might be a good thing, because they won the Ivy League, but by virtue of winning the league through miraculous measures, it may have raised the expectations higher than they should be. Penn will be out to prove that it didn’t merely catch lightning in a bottle in Ithaca. X-FACTOR: AJ Levine. What is the ceiling for AJ Levine? He’s already one of the best guards in the Ivy League on the defensive end, but without Ethan Roberts, he’ll have to shoulder a bigger role on offense. Can he step up as a scorer to give another element to this group? 2. YALE WHAT I LIKE: James Jones has never really needed to rebuild since COVID. He’s always found his next star waiting in the wings. Trevor Mullin and Riley Fox are the obvious candidates this season. Mullin started at the point for the Bulldogs last year and is an efficient outside shooter who doesn’t turn the ball over much. He’ll need to take a big step forward though. Fox is arguably the Ivy League’s best shooter. The 6-foot-6 sniper shot 37% on four attempts per game last year

PENN WHAT I LIKE: The Quakers return most of their rotation pieces from the squad that shocked the world and won Ivy Madness last year. That all starts with TJ Power, whose 44-point miracle performance against Yale stands as one of the league’s greatest ever. He’s a legit three-level scoring superstar in the Ivy League, and at 6-foot-8, he’s a mismatch nightmare for opponents. One of the league’s deadliest shooters, Mike Zanoni, returns alongside him. Notre Dame transfer Sir Mohammed adds a little bit of physicality on the wing, something that Penn desperately needs. There’s depth in the frontcourt with the returning Dalton Scantlebury/Augie Gerhart duo. Both are skilled post scorers, and I think Scantlebury could eventually leapfrog Gerhart in the rotation. Lucas Lueth also gives the Quakers some rim protection and athleticism up front, although he’s more a four than five. WHAT I DON’T LIKE: Penn’s analytical profile relies a ton on mid-range jump shots. The Quakers didn’t get to the rim at a high enough rate last year and are one of the few teams that still consistently runs actions for long twos. Penn will have the same strengths and weaknesses as last season. That might be a good thing, because they won the Ivy League, but by virtue of winning the league through miraculous measures, it may have raised the expectations higher than they should be. Penn will be out to prove that it didn’t merely catch lightning in a bottle in Ithaca. X-FACTOR: AJ Levine. What is the ceiling for AJ Levine? He’s already one of the best guards in the Ivy League on the defensive end, but without Ethan Roberts, he’ll have to shoulder a bigger role on offense. Can he step up as a scorer to give another element to this group? 2. YALE WHAT I LIKE: James Jones has never really needed to rebuild since COVID. He’s always found his next star waiting in the wings. Trevor Mullin and Riley Fox are the obvious candidates this season. Mullin started at the point for the Bulldogs last year and is an efficient outside shooter who doesn’t turn the ball over much. He’ll need to take a big step forward though. Fox is arguably the Ivy League’s best shooter. The 6-foot-6 sniper shot 37% on four attempts per game last year and will probably take way more than that this season. Jordan Brathwaite also is back, another stellar shooter who will make this one of the most dynamic shooting teams in the league. WHAT I DON’T LIKE: Despite those two players, this is probably the weakest Yale returning crop in some time. After losing Samson Aletan a year early and Isaac Celiscar two years early, the Buldogs are relying on a lot of players who haven’t proven anything at all. Courtney Wallace and Daniel Ogunyemi have potential but haven’t shown much. Wallace’s athleticism could be a major piece for a backcourt that lacks the level of athleticism that it has had over the past few years. Division-III transfer Connor May will also play a role with his shooting. X-FACTOR: Jack Sullivan. Yale has not finished outside the top 2 in defense in the Ivy League since before COVID. If the Bulldogs do it again, Sullivan must be an excellent rim protector. The 6-foot-11 sophomore didn’t play much last year, but the keys to the season are in his hands. 3. HARVARD WHAT I LIKE: The returning trio of Rob Hinton, Tey Barbour and Thomas Batties II is the best in the Ivy League. Hinton is arguably the most talented player in the conference as a 6-foot-5 jumbo creator that gets to his spots and scores at a high level. He must take a step forward as a playmaker and shooter this year, but the talent is there. Barbour and Batties were knockdown shooters last season, while Batties provided interior rim protection. Ben Eisendrath was a pesky player off the ball, and a healthy Austin Hunt could make a big difference as well. WHAT I DON’T LIKE: I don’t think people talked enough about how much Chandler Piggé did for the Crimson last year. He was the glue guy on both ends who made that team work. Perhaps Hunt can bring some of that back without Piggé this year. Additionally, it’s harder to trust Tommy Amaker than it was 10 years ago. A coaching gap might be the difference between the Crimson and the two teams above them. With the same strengths and weaknesses as last year, unless Harvard finds more production outside of its stars, it could limit the ceiling. X-FACTOR: Freshman class. The Crimson once again have a loaded freshman group. Jason Singleton and Preston Merrick are athletic players who can impact the game by pushing the pace for Harvard, an element that the team didn’t have last year. Singleton seems like the most important piece, as a highly-touted combo guard with scoring chops. Merrick is more of an off-ball runner type. PRINCETON WHAT I LIKE: Princeton returns the entire rotation from last season. When you run a Princeton-style offense, continuity and familiarity is extremely important. It’s not just the starting group. It’s everybody. Jack Stanton, Malik Abdullahi and CJ Happy are now upperclassmen. Dalen Davis, Jackson Hicke and Jacob Huggins are seniors. They’ve all been through the battles in this system. They’ve all had their bouts with inconsistency but have shown the ability to be the guy on a given night. Stanton returning from injury after missing the final stretch of the season will be a huge boon to the offense as he’s an elite shooter. Hicke took a huge step last year as well. I really liked what Landon Clark gave the Tigers last season, and as a sophomore, he could be a key glue guy. WHAT I DON’T LIKE: Last year was the worst Princeton team that Mitch Henderson fielded as Tiger head coach. They finished with a losing Ivy record for the second time in his tenure and failed to crack double-digit wins for the first time since 2007-08. As I’ve said with Penn and Harvard, when you retain as much, you don’t just retain the strengths, but also the weaknesses. There aren’t a lot of great individual defenders on this roster, and Princeton was the worst defensive rebounding team in the Ivy League last year, which is a far cry from a program strength. X-FACTOR: Dalen Davis is Princeton’s most talented offensive player. He needs to be consistent on that end this year. The Tigers will not be able to afford sinking 30% usage rates into him if he’s putting up a 99.2 offensive rating again this year. He doesn’t have to be the best player on the floor every night, but he has to be able to pick and choose his spots. 5. CORNELL WHAT I LIKE: The backcourt has a lot of fun pieces. Jacob Beccles is in line to be Cornell’s next All-Ivy guard as a senior. Each year, he’s gotten more decisive and aggressive and provides positional size and physicality to score inside and out. Anthony Nimani is also poised for a big season with a bigger role, while Mateen Rafiq might be the biggest upside piece for the Big Red as he sees more playing time. First, it’s Ben Johnson’s offense and play calling, which everyone in the league knows is elite. But if the play Johnson calls doesn’t have it, the defense still has to deal with what Caleb Williams can do when the play breaks down. The Bears offense has a chance to really hit some great heights this year with the synergy that Ben and Caleb are developing. 2. How will not having Kyle Monangai affect the Bears’ offense? Who would be the next men up? Monangai missing is definitely a knock to the offense. He and D’Andre Swift make a great combination, and they complement each other well. Roschon Johnson would be the guy to fill in. Johnson doesn’t have the speed or shiftiness of Monangai. There are fans I know that call him SlowJo instead of RoJo. He had just 6 yards on five attempts against Green Bay, and last week he was much better with 51 yards on 13 carries, but that still keeps him below the 4.0 threshold. Johnson is a nice blocker, has pretty good hands, and is a good special teamer. But he’s not a guy you want having 10-plus touches in a game. 3. The Bears have been one of the league’s worst deep pass defenses, but their corners seem to be getting healthy. What’s behind those struggles and how much would having all three starters affect Chicago’s ability to defend deep? What’s behind the Bears’ lack of success from their secondary? I mean, should I say lack of talent? With Kyler Gordon out, the Bears were mostly running out Jaylon Johnson, Tyrique Stevenson, and rookie Malik Muhammad. With Gordon back last week, they have moved Muhammad to play more outside and made them less reliant on the other two. Reports were really good over the summer that Johnson had recovered from the injuries that plagued him in 2025, and he was back to his old form. That really hasn’t been the case. Stevenson can make plays as well because he’s a pretty aggressive corner. Having Gordon back gives them a great blitzing weapon and great play at the line of scrimmage, and his presence will limit how much someone like Stevenson has to be on the field. That will help in some regards, but the Bears are going to be susceptible to the deep ball against Drake Maye for sure. 4. What’s makes the Bears such an effective blitzing defense? Has anyone managed to slow them down? The key to the Bears blitzing is the success they are having with it on third down. The Bears have 17 sacks on the season; nine of them have come on third down. That makes them arguably the best third-down defense in the NFL. Heading into this game, opponents have converted just 26% of their third downs against the Bears, trailing only the Minnesota Vikings. Defensive Coordinator Dennis Allen has been a wizard with this team on third downs, and that’s not just last year; they were good on third downs last year as well, despite being one of the worst overall defenses in the league. What’s wild about those nine third-down sacks I mentioned earlier, four have come from defensive backs. You can expect Kyler Gordon to blitz frequently, and with the banged-up Patriots offensive line, it wouldn’t shock me if he gets home for another sack on Thursday night. Even in the Bears’ losses, the third-down conversion rates sit at 7-for-25, so still close to their averages. It sounds dumb, but the best way to beat the Bears’ third-down success? Stay out of third and long. The Bears can be had on first and second down, so gain yards there, avoid third downs all together or at least keep it to third and short where it’s a quick-hitting play and the blitz doesn’t have a chance to get home. 5. Who do you think pulls out a victory on Thursday night, and why? I do think the Bears are going to win this one. I think they are carrying a lot of momentum and confidence with Caleb Williams back. I think the offense is clicking, and I do think the Patriots’ defense can cause some issues for them, but I do think they can score on them. I expect Drake Maye to beat the Bears with a few pretty deep balls, but I do think they will make some plays on third down and stop enough Patriots drives. Thursday games are tricky because they always seem like anything can happen with a short week of preparation. These are two good football teams, so we should expect a close game. Bears 27, Patriots 24.

item.title: Steve Kerr caught on hot mic calling out Lakers double standards
item.description: Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images Steve Kerr didn’t realise his mic was still hot, but fans certainly heard him loud and clear as he vented his frustration over how refs whistle games in Los Angeles. The Golden State Warriors suffered a rough 127-105 blowout loss to the Los Angeles Lakers, with familiar officiating frustrations boiling over once again. Fans and players vented over Luka Doncic’s whistle advantage, calling out his constant foul-baiting and whining to the refs after every drive. The Lakers shot 24-of-27 from the free throw line on 25 personal fouls called against Golden State. Meanwhile, the Warriors shot 21-of-27 from the charity stripe on 19 fouls called against LA. Steve Kerr warns Yaxel Lendeborg about refereeing vs Lakers Steve Kerr didn’t realise the broadcast mics were picking up every word when he leaned in to talk to Yaxel Lendeborg on the sideline. Trailing by 22 in the third quarter, Kerr vented his frustration right into the mic, complaining about the soft whistle the Lakers were getting at home. Shown live on ESPN, Brick Center shared the video, where Kerr said: “They call all that s*** here, they wouldn’t call it in any other arena.” Kerr’s hot mic frustration matches what Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg experienced directly on the court. After guarding Luka Doncic, Lendeborg admitted he lost all respect for the star , calling out his non-stop flopping, whining to refs, and the soft calls that left Golden State defenseless. item.title: Pirates Minor League Awards: Gray Top Player, Hernandez Top Pitcher
item.description: The Pirates spent the week announcing their 2026 minor-league award winners. Murf Gray was named the Honus Wagner Player of the Year and Seth Hernandez was named the Bob Friend Pitcher of the Year. Gray, who also won the Wille Stargell Slugger of the Year, skyrocketed up the system in his first professional season. The 22-year-old began the season with Low-A Bradenton and ended the year in Double-A Altoona. He combined to slash .305/.402/.567 with 27 doubles, 32 home runs and 97 RBI across three levels. Gray, who was drafted by the Pirates in the second round in 2025, led Pittsburgh’s minor league players in hits (143), home runs, RBI, slugging percentage, runs (100), extra-base hits (59) and total bases (266). Hernandez split the year between Bradenton and High-A Greensboro. The ’25 first-round draft pick combined to go 6-1 with a 2.43 ERA in 18 starts. He logged 74 innings, walked 31, struck out 118 and held opponents to a .181 batting average. Hernandez, 20, was placed on the injured list with a season-ending oblique strain on July 25. At the time he landed on the IL, the right-hander was second among all minor-league pitchers in strikeouts. Both Gray (89) and Hernandez (nine) are considered top 100 prospect by MLB Pipeline. Gray is considered the third-best third base prospect. Hernandez is ranked as the top right-hander pitcher. Other Pirates Minor-League Awards Jesus Castillo was named the Bill Mazeroski Defender of the Year. Castillo played every position other than pitcher and catcher in 2026 and committed just nine errors in 288 chances. Yordany De Los Santos won the Omar Moreno Baserunner of the Year after leading the organization with 45 stolen bases in 92 games split between Bradenton and Greensboro. Right-hander Derek Diamond was named the Kent Tekulve Reliever of the Year. Diamond went 7-0 with a 2.45 ERA and a pair of saves in 37 appearances, 29 of which were with Triple-A Indianapolis. Johan De Los Santos was named the Pirates’ rookie level player of the year. The 18-year-old combined to slash .310/.431/.434 with four triples, two home runs, 10 RBI and 26 steals in 31 FCL games before a promotion to Bradenton. Irwin Ramirez was tabbed as the Pirates’ top rookie level pitcher. The right-hander went 1-1 with a 3.67 ERA in eight starts in the Florida Complex League before a promotion to Bradenton. He held opponents to a .157 batting average. The Pirates named Cecilio Beltre as the organization’s staff member of the year. He was a team development coach/mentor for the Dominican Summer League Pirates Gold team. item.title: Hornell's Mehr named Buffalo Bills Coach of the Week after big win
item.description: The Hornell/Arkport-Canaseraga football program is enjoying a strong 2026 campaign, and the Buffalo Bills have taken notice. Hornell/A-C head coach Dr. Ismail Mehr has been named one of the 2026 High School Tackle Football Coaches of the Week by the Buffalo Bills in partnership with Visa. Mehr was named the Rochester Coach of the Week by the Bills, while the Buffalo Region Coach of the Week was Chad Bartoszek of Salamanca. The weekly honor by the Bills aims to highlight football coaches' efforts on and off the field, recognizing their team's excellence on the field and their service to their communities. As part of the program, each winning coach's program will receive $1,000 from the Buffalo Bills and Visa, and each region's Coach of the Year will receive an additional $1,000 and be celebrated on the field at Highmark Stadium before the Bills vs. Jets game in January. Mehr was honored after leading the Red Raiders to a 19-13 victory over previously undefeated Alexander/Pembroke that moved Hornell/A-C to 6-1 on the season. Tyrone Buchanan sealed the win with a rushing touchdown with under five minutes left in the fourth quarter. Senior running back Matt Karr powered the running game, rushing 12 times for 147 yards and a touchdown. Mehr has been a part of Hornell football for more than two decades, noted the Bills. A 1991 Hornell High School graduate, he returned to his hometown in 2002 after completing medical school and specializing in anesthesiology. He is a board-certified anesthesiologist and medical director at UR Medicine St. James Hospital in Hornell. He began his coaching career as an assistant on the staff of legendary Hornell football coach Gene Mastin . More: Where does Hornell's Mastin now rank after new Section V wins record After years of serving as an assistant coach, Mehr took over as head coach and has led the Red Raiders for the past four seasons. "Community involvement is an important part of the Hornell football program," Mehr told the Bills. "Hornell is a small, blue-collar, hard-working community, and the football program believes strongly in giving back to the community that supports it. As a staff, we encourage our players to be active, responsible, and proud members of the community." The move follows a post published by the La Liga president on X on 16 October, with the CSD asking the independent tribunal to assess whether his remarks could constitute a serious sporting offence. Tebas, who also serves as a vice-president of the Spanish Football Federation (RFEF), made the comparison while criticising Real Madrid’s media approach. The CSD has acted on its own initiative, submitting a reasoned request for the TAD to examine the matter. CSD asks TAD to assess whether Tebas breached Spanish sports law In its statement, the CSD said it had submitted the request because of Tebas’s remarks about Real Madrid. According to the council, the league president compared the club’s communication methods to the “propaganda mechanisms exploited by Goebbels, Minister of Propaganda in Nazi Germany.” CSD statement on Tebas’ comments against Real Madrid. The CSD has asked the TAD to determine whether the comments show evidence of a possible breach of Article 76.4.b of Spain’s Sports Law 10/1990. item.title: Bernardo Silva: “I am very happy to have scored my first goal with this jersey”
item.description: Real Madrid midfielder Bernardo Silva scored the team’s opening goal against Red Bull Leipzig, his first goal as a madridista, and talked to the club’s media after the game. “I am very happy to have won this game and scored my first goal with this jersey. It was a tough match, where I think we were much better in the second half than in the first. In the first half, we created some chances but also allowed them to approach our goal quite a bit. Thibaut was very important for us. In the second half, we controlled the game much better, and in the end, we secured a good victory. We are happy and will keep moving forward,” he said. Bernardo also explained what Mourinho wants from the midfielders. “It doesn’t matter who is on the pitch. We are a team with very aggressive and strong players in one-on-one situations, who love dribbling and making runs into space. We need to find the balance between maintaining possession, finding the forwards, and being direct. We want to play fluid football, and we are getting to know each other better and trying to improve. I think the team has improved a lot in recent games, and I’m sure it will continue to do so soon. We need to strike that balance between controlling possession and the game while also not being a boring team, staying intense and aggressive, as Real Madrid has always been. That’s difficult, and you need to be very prepared to do it well,” he added. He also talked about his role. “I keep working. I’m ready to help this club. Whether it’s one minute, five, ten, or ninety… I’ll be training well, helping the group, and the day the coach feels he needs me, I’ll be ready,” he explained.

item.title: 3 Players Heat Traded Lead Bucks in Scoring in Opener
item.description: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - OCTOBER 16: Tyler Herro #11of the Milwaukee Bucks dribbles the ball against the Indiana Pacers at Gainbridge Fieldhouse on October 16, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) Getty The Milwaukee Bucks started a new era on Wednesday night — the post-Giannis Antetokounmpo period of the franchise. It’s a painful reality to face, that the best player to ever don a Bucks uniform is gone, traded to the Miami Heat. All the Bucks can do is move forward, and they didn’t get off to a great start of that with a 128-116 loss to the Washington Wizards to open their season on Wednesday. There were positive signs, though, mostly coming from the players they got in return for Giannis. In fact, three of the trade return players were the three-leading scorers for the Bucks on Wednesday. And for what it’s worth, the Heat lost their opener to, falling to the Minnesota Timberwolves . So improvements can be made all around. Tyler Herro Debut Tyler Herro is a Milwaukee-native, so it’s got to be special for him to get to play for the Bucks. Wednesday’s game was on the road, not yet home cooking for Herro, but he did lead Milwaukee in scoring. Herro put up 24 points on 9-for-21 from the floor, including 4-for-11 from 3, while making both his attempted foul shots. Herro added nine assists, two rebounds and a steal while turning the ball over four times. He’s going to have to lead the Bucks in scoring most nights to have a chance. Jaime Jaquez The forward Jaime Jaquez had a great Bucks debut after coming over in the Giannis trade. He put up 22 points on 8-for-12 from the field, including 1-for-3 from 3, and made 5-of-6 free throws. Jaquez also had seven rebounds and two assists while turning it over twice. He was the only member of the Bucks without a negative plus-minus (his was actually 0). Kasparas Jakucionis Jakucionis was just drafted in 2025, but he had a great start for the Bucks after the trade. He put up 15 points on 4-for-7 shooting, including 1-for-3 from 3, while making all six of his foul shots. Jakucionis added three rebounds and three assists with one block and one turnover. Kel’el Ware Ware was the quietest player to have arrived in the Giannis trade. He got 14 minutes off the bench and put up seven points with three rebounds, one assist, one steal and one turnover. Ware was 3-for-6 from the floor, but 0-for-2 from 3 and 1-for-3 from the foul line. It could be tough for Ware to play much more in the early going with Jaquez, Kyle Kuzma and Myles Turner all in the starting lineup, and on Wednesday, Ousmane Dieng got more minutes off the bench, too. However, this report was officially retracted on October 20 by The Times who conceded that FIFA's report did not disclose this additional income because Swiss tax law rules do not count expense and reimbursement payments as compensation with regards to filings and reportings by non-profits. They also acknowledged that claims regarding a Miami property purchase were false. FIFA assert that Infantino's payments from FWC2026 were not part of his regular salary or compensation, and therefore were not required to be disclosed in their annual report by Swiss tax law, and therefore, while included in the U.S. tax filings, were not required to be publicly announced. FIFA & FIFA PRESIDENT RECEIVES APOLOGY FROM ‘THE TIMES’ FIFA takes note of an apology published today by The Times following an inaccurate and damaging report: On 13 October 2026 (Sport), we reported that Gianni Infantino received a "second salary" from Fifa, which Fifa had failed to disclose. This is incorrect. There was no “second salary.” Regulations do not require Fifa to include expenses and reimbursements received by Mr Infantino in its annual report as they are not considered "compensation" under Swiss reporting requirements. We also accept Mr Infantino did not purchase a property in Miami at a suspected undervalue as we reported and neither he nor his family are the legal or beneficial owners of Shadi LLC and have no control over that company, as we suggested. We are happy to make these corrections and apologise to Mr Infantino and Fifa for the errors. As FIFA stated in August, it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its President. FIFA urges the media to act responsibly and carefully verify all sourcing to prevent the publication and subsequent reproduction of false and defamatory information. FIFA welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a license to amplify false allegations. Where reporting is inaccurate, misleading, or totally false, as in this case, FIFA will continue to challenge it directly and vigorously. — FIFA Media (@fifamedia) October 20, 2026 Following the retraction, FIFA acknowledged the apology they received from The Times and warned there was a "concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its President."

item.description: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Mike Sullivan apparently heard the outside noise and wanted to set the record straight about certain poor underlying metrics for the New York Rangers defensemen so far this season. As reported in several spaces, including here in a recent article published by Tom Castro , the Rangers spend a lot of time defending, are being out-chanced, and have a mediocre expected goal share — collectively as a team, and individually by player. Castro pointed these things out, backed up by underlying metrics from Natural Stat Trick , and stated that it’s something the Rangers should have some level of concern about. Of course, the Rangers are 7-3-1 to start the season and certainly pass the eye test in most areas of their play. Their defensive zone exits are much crisper and cleaner, and the support and structure sure appear better than in previous seasons. A big part of that is that New York works much better now in five-man groups with the forwards much more dedicated to playing a 200-foot game, which Castro rightly pointed out. But Sullivan also correctly argued that one can’t simply look at any one stat or underlying metric in a vacuum to form a complete opinion. “When you start looking at metrics and things of that nature, context is really important. If you don’t understand context, it’s hard for you to interpret data the right way,” the Rangers coach said Wednesday . “So for example, if there’s a defense pair or a line combination that gets a lot of defensive-zone starts against the other team’s top players, they’re probably going to be on the ice for some chances against. But they might limit the quality of the chance or the quantity of the chances of the other team’s top players, and they keep them off the board, and we have success because of it. Their metrics might not look positive, but the value is they help us win.” Specifically speaking about the team’s new second defense pairing of Marcus Pettersson and Sean Durzi , there’s no question the Rangers are much better off with those two veterans in that role than any combinations they put together in recent years. I pointed to that is the Rangers Daily column on Wednesday. “When you look at multiple data points, it gives you a little bit of a better picture of what that context is or what it looks like. So, we believe Marcus and ‘Durz’ have given us pretty good minutes,” Sullivan explained. “Some nights they’ve been better than others, without a doubt. But I also think there’s more to it than (the analytics).” Fair enough. Analytics are important. So, too, are results, the eye test, the human element. That’s why the Yankees bringing back the analytics-driven Aaron Boone as manager draws so much criticism from fans and reporters alike, because it’s so one-sided how he runs that team and goes about making his decisions. Sully appears to have a good balance of both in how he oversees the Rangers. New York Rangers news and analysis Brad Penner-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IM

As Delap prepares to return to Ipswich, where his career ignited, on Friday night, Forest are remaining calm. There is a desperation to get away from the short-termism that caused so many problems; 12 months ago, they were on their third head coach of a disappointing season. This summer they were ruthless with the removal of Vítor Pereira, who had done a fine job to escape the drop, because they saw an opportunity to upgrade with Glasner, hoping he could transform Forest like he did Crystal Palace. item.title: Barkley and Buendía on target as Aston Villa sink Viking to maintain perfect start
item.description: For a little over 20 minutes, Aston Villa could look down on the rest of Europe. They had scaled the Champions League summit on goal difference when Henrik Heggheim put through his own net and the fact was not lost on the Holte End, who reflected their position in song and perhaps allowed themselves another glimpse back to the days when their supremacy was undisputed. “We’ve conquered before, we’re prepared for more,” the pre-match tifo display had read. Perhaps Villa really will rekindle the spirit of 1982 but the frustration here, albeit minor in the wider scheme, was that they could not maintain their bird’s-eye view over the continent. A superbly taken volley by Peter Christiansen, awarded by the video assistant referee after initially being disallowed for offside, gave Viking a consolation their second-half display deserved and meant Unai Emery’s side must make do with slumming it just behind Paris Saint-Germain. item.title: Manchester City have been a joy to watch but they became detached from their roots | Philipp Lahm
item.description: City behaved much like other top clubs but their rule-breaking deserves to be punished. The Bundesliga, where members have a controlling stake, can show the way forward Do we have to reassess Manchester City now? In my columns, I have repeatedly engaged with this club and its key figures. Looking back at what I have written over the years, I believe it remains beyond question that the team have achieved greatness. I always loved watching them: they were a true unit on the pitch, a finely tuned orchestra. I would also write all over again that the conductor, Pep Guardiola, masters his craft like few others. I could recognise his teams even if they were wearing the wrong shirts and the game was broadcast in black and white – by the passes, the distances between the players and the intelligence of their interplay. It is no wonder Guardiola inspires others to become managers; look at Vincent Kompany, Mikel Arteta, Enzo Maresca, and perhaps some time Ilkay Gündogan and Rodri. Continue reading...

item.title: Too much Overlap? Gary Neville’s podcast empire knows no bounds
item.description: The Overlap has gone daily, with Steven Gerrard and Joe Hart among the latest additions to an ever-growing family Viewed in 2026, Nathan Barley, Chris Morris’s 2005 sitcom, shows remarkable prescience about the last two decades of metropolitan life, from smartphone addiction and digital derangement to sheer existential vapidity. When Barley’s character referred to his occupation as “self-facilitating media node”, Morris and co-writer Charlie Brooker were way ahead on the creator economy. What the pair failed to predict was ex-footballers joining the sector in droves. These days, if you are a former footballer without a podcast or YouTube channel, then did you ever really play the game? Setting aside the Gary Lineker Goalhanger empire, manspreading its centrist-dad agenda into issues way beyond guffaws with Micah Richards and Alan Shearer, there is Gary Neville to rule them all. Manchesterism’s second-most influential practitioner has been on heavy manoeuvres. Unlike Lineker’s productions, the Overlap’s output continues to stick largely to football; a rugby podcast was mothballed in February, though its cricket equivalent continues. Continue reading...

item.description: The 19-year-old scored a cracker in Seville, days after his ‘almost rabona’ at Galatasaray, as La Liga leaders beat Real Betis When at last it was time for Lamine Yamal to leave, the 19-year-old’s number going up before the 90th minute for only the second time since the opening day, Real Betis fans whistled him all the way to the touchline where Barcelona’s coach was waiting. His work here was done, Hansi Flick invited him to take the weight off his feet and his shoulders, not that he wanted to. First, though, he took Lamine Yamal’s head in his hands and, leaning in away from the amateur lip readers, tried to make himself heard over the noise. “I told him I was proud of him because he played a fantastic game,” he said. At least he could think of something. When Lamine Yamal had opened the scoring just nine minutes into the match that was supposed to find out how good Barcelona really were, it hadn’t been easy. Nothing erudite, anyway. On the morning that Barcelona went to Betis – first v third, a proper opponent at last – Jorge Valdano had lamented that sometimes he doesn’t have the words, and he always has the words. Valdano had just watched Lamine do that , whatever that was , in Istanbul – an “almost rabona ”, the kid called it – and now he had a problem. “If he keeps doing strange things, we’re not going to be able to explain it,” he wrote . item.title: Brighton are the apex B club – their next target should be a Champions League place | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: Diego Gómez’s wondergoal in a five-star demolition is just the latest in an impressive run of results for the south coast team Sign up for our free newsletter here For two or three years now, it’s been standard to nod approvingly at how well-run Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth are, and to move on. What else is there to say? It’s true, of course – these are sides who have made the most of relatively limited resources. But there’s also an underlying assumption in the designation: that these are clubs who have no higher aspiration, that their limit is earning praise for upper mid-table finishes. This season, perhaps, offers an opportunity to change that. Other than Arsenal, every major club is undergoing significant transition. Manchester City may have started the season with seven straight wins, but there’s every chance the punishment for their multiple breaches of Premier League regulations takes them out of the race for the top five. In that context, why shouldn’t one of those efficient smaller sides qualify for the Champions League? Continue reading...

item.description: Another round of games and another disappointing draw for Arsenal while Manchester City sit top of the table with a 100% record There would have been hope that the international break could offer the Arsenal players and staff a reset but the same problems reared their head at the Emirates on Sunday in a 1-1 draw with Birmingham. As they have done so often this season, the Gunners dominated most attacking and possession-based metrics – they registered 76% possession, a 2.73 xG and 43 touches in the opposition box – but their profligacy in front of goal and lack of urgency in their play once again came to the fore. Of their 27 chances, they managed just four on target as they toiled against a resilient opposition who understood the playbook. Birmingham set up in a strong defensive structure, protecting their box admirably with numbers to frustrate Renée Slegers’s side, who famously struggle to break down low blocks. item.title: Europe is a blast – but more a curse than a blessing if you are not a Premier League super-club I Jonathan Wilson
item.description: The four Premier League clubs playing in the lesser continental competitions face each other on Sunday – but three are struggling domestically The sun shone. The temperature was in the high 20s. There was a mood of great conviviality. If you were struggling with the official allocation, it turned out you could just email the president of Torreense and he’d sort you out. Were these “Nuno-tickets” real? It turned out they were. Not only that, but you could sit anywhere you wanted in a stadium too big for the game and, if you happened to have gravitated to the comfortable hospitality seating at the back of the lower tier, the beer was inexplicably free. Locals in Leiria seemed bewildered but could hardly have been more accommodating. A beer pump had been installed outside a patisserie on the Praça Francisco Rodrigues Lobo, whose owner soon found fans happy to help stack empty barrels if that facilitated the free flow of Sagres. “There was a meeting at the town hall to explain these are not hooligans,” said the owner of a radical leftist flammkuchen restaurant between the square and the cathedral. “They told us the club comes from the labour movement and I found that very interesting.” And how had she found the fans? “Noisy, but with a quirky sense of humour.” Continue reading...

item.title: Houthi conflict casts shadow as Saudi Arabia scales back sporting pipe dreams
item.description: A match delayed by missile attack warnings is not what Cristiano Ronaldo and co signed up for but it’s the new reality; the Saudi sporting juggernaut is stalling Cristiano Ronaldo grabbed the scarf in the colours of the Saudi Arabian flag and waved it at the sparse but enthusiastic crowd, who responded with rapturous cheers. It was a gesture of defiance rather than a victory salute, encapsulating the Saudi equivalent of “Keep calm and carry on”. Monday night’s Asian Champions League Elite game between Al-Nassr and the Uzbek side Neftchi Fergana had ended with a 3-1 win for the Saudi club coached by Ange Postecoglou, with Ronaldo, supported by Sadio Mané, scoring, the smattering of star names indicative of the lure of the Saudi Pro League. Yet this isn’t quite how Ronaldo and co would have anticipated life in Riyadh. The meagre attendance aside, Monday’s game was delayed by a threat of missile attacks from Yemen’s Houthi rebels. A safety warning issued 15 minutes before kick-off came two days after 13 people died and more than 300 were wounded by Houthi strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport. item.title: James McClean: ‘Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen’
item.description: The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career “The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.” McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. I played 150 Premier League games over five seasons, 800 professional games and won a lot of individual accolades. I count that as success and don’t look back with regrets.” Continue reading...

item.title: The Premier League so far: draws, underperforming xG and other data pointers
item.description: Goal averages are crumbling as players take fewer touches in the box and forwards underperform against xG Goals are on the up in the Premier League. The average of 2.70 non-penalty goals per game in 2026-27 is higher than last season and two of the four previous campaigns. Yet we should have been even more royally entertained. Matches have averaged 2.88 non-penalty expected goals, the second most in the past six seasons. Chances have been going to waste. If the 20 teams converted at the par rate, there would have been almost two extra goals per week. As few as that sounds, the proportion of games drawn is higher than in any past Premier League season. Some tied matches might have been settled had the finishing been up to the mark. item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...
